chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Optimization Theory Matters for Portfolio Construction

lessons.title: From Markowitz to the Math: Portfolio Construction as a Constrained Optimization Problem

children.text: The interviewer is not done with Ananya. Good, he says, you can state the minimum variance problem for a fixed set of weights. Now generalize it. I want the entire efficient frontier, not one portfolio. For any expected return I name, give me the portfolio with the lowest possible variance that hits it exactly. Ananya realizes this is not a new problem. It is the same three ingredients from the last lesson, decision variables, objective function, constraints, with one more constraint added. If you have taken a Markowitz-focused course before, this lesson is the bridge between the efficient frontier you already know and the optimization language the rest of this course runs on.

body.text: The Markowitz efficient frontier is not a separate topic from optimization theory. It is a single named example of a constrained optimization problem: minimize a quadratic objective, portfolio variance, subject to linear constraints, a target return and a budget rule.

children.text: Recap: Portfolio Return and Portfolio Variance in Vector Form

Two quantities drive every portfolio construction problem: how much return you expect to earn, and how much risk you take to earn it. In vector notation, with w as the vector of portfolio weights, mu as the vector of expected returns for each stock, and Sigma as the covariance matrix of returns:

body.caption: Portfolio expected return: a weighted average of individual expected returns.
Portfolio variance: the same expression introduced in the previous lesson.

children.text: The Full Constrained Optimization Statement of Markowitz

markDefs.definition: The curve traced by plotting, for every achievable target return, the single portfolio with the lowest possible variance that hits it. Each point on the curve is the solution to one instance of the optimization problem below, solved at a different target return.

children.text: , you pick a target return, call it R*, and solve this problem once. Then you change R* and solve it again. Repeat enough times and the solutions trace out the entire frontier.

body.caption: Constraint 1: hit the target return exactly.
Constraint 2: the budget rule. Weights add up to 1, every rupee allocated.

children.text: Two Equivalent Framings of the Same Frontier

You can walk the same frontier from either direction: fix a target return and minimize variance, or fix a target variance and maximize return. Both produce identical frontier portfolios, just parameterized differently.

body.caption: Two ways to state the same efficient frontier problem
headers: Minimize Variance for a Target Return
Maximize Return for a Target Variance

cells: Constraints: wᵀμ = R*, sum of w = 1
Constraints: wᵀΣw = σ*², sum of w = 1

children.text: Why This Problem Type Has a Name: Quadratic Programs

markDefs.definition: An optimization problem whose objective function is quadratic (built from squared and cross-product terms of the decision variables) and whose constraints are linear. Portfolio variance minimization is a textbook quadratic program.

children.text: Portfolio variance, wᵀΣw, is a quadratic function of the weights: expand it and every term is either a weight squared or a product of two weights. The return and budget constraints are both linear: no weight is squared or multiplied by another. An optimization problem built from a quadratic objective and linear constraints has a standard name, a

, usually shortened to QP. This is not just terminology. Recognizing a problem as a QP tells you immediately which solution methods apply, and, as Chapter 2 shows, whether the problem behaves well enough to guarantee a solution at all.

body.label: Markowitz's optimization problem
body.context: Convex because the covariance matrix Sigma, built from real variances and covariances, guarantees the objective curves upward in every direction, never downward. Chapter 2 makes this precise.

body.text: Not every optimization problem you will meet in quant finance is this well-behaved. Some objectives have multiple local minima, where a solver can get stuck at an answer that looks optimal locally but is not the best one available. Convex QPs like this one do not have that problem: any local minimum you find is guaranteed to be the global minimum. That guarantee is the entire subject of Chapter 2.

children.text: Case Study: Writing Ananya's Three-Stock Problem in Full
Return to Reliance Industries, TCS, and HDFC Bank from the previous lesson, now with illustrative numbers attached, and a target return of exactly 15%.

body.caption: Illustrative annualized covariance matrix (decimal, rounded to 4 places)

children.text: Diagonal entries are each stock's own variance (volatility squared: 0.28² = 0.0784 for Reliance). Off-diagonal entries are covariances between pairs. With these numbers and a 15% target return, the full problem is:

body.caption: The objective, fully expanded from wᵀΣw using the covariance matrix above.
Both constraints, the return target and the budget rule, written with the actual numbers.

body.title: Show me the expansion from wᵀΣw

children.text: Multiplying out wᵀΣw for three assets gives each weight squared times its own variance, plus twice each pairwise weight product times the corresponding covariance, since Sigma is symmetric and each off-diagonal term appears twice.

content.caption: The general pattern behind the expanded objective above. It scales to any number of assets without changing shape.

body.text: Count the pieces: 3 decision variables (w1, w2, w3), 2 equality constraints (return target, budget). That leaves only 1 degree of freedom. With just one free direction to search, you could almost eyeball this one. Scale up to 30 or 300 stocks and that stops being true. Chapter 4 builds the tool, Lagrange multipliers, that finds the exact answer regardless of how many degrees of freedom remain.

body.title: Translate the scenario
body.scenario: A wealth manager tells a client: I want the portfolio with the lowest possible volatility, targeting an expected return of exactly 12%, using only these four Nifty 50 stocks, with every rupee invested and none held back.
body.prompt: Write this as a constrained optimization problem. State the decision variables, the objective function, and every constraint.
body.modelAnswer: Decision variables: w1, w2, w3, w4, the weights on the four stocks. Objective: minimize wᵀΣw (portfolio variance). Constraints: wᵀμ = 0.12 (expected return hits exactly 12%) and w1 + w2 + w3 + w4 = 1 (fully invested, no leverage, no cash held back).

body.title: Count the constraints
body.question: You are given a portfolio problem with 6 stocks: minimize variance, subject to a target return of 18% and full investment (weights sum to 1). How many decision variables and how many equality constraints does this problem have?
body.explanation: There are 6 decision variables, one weight per stock. There are 2 equality constraints: the target return constraint and the budget constraint. That leaves 6 minus 2, or 4, degrees of freedom, far too many to solve by inspection, which is exactly what Lagrange multipliers in Chapter 4 are built to handle systematically.

points: The Markowitz efficient frontier problem is a specific instance of constrained optimization: minimize a quadratic objective, portfolio variance, subject to linear constraints, a target return and a budget rule.
Sweeping the target return R* across its achievable range and solving the minimum-variance problem at each value is literally how the efficient frontier gets traced.
Because the objective is quadratic and the constraints are linear, this class of problem is called a quadratic program (QP). Markowitz's version of it is convex.

Each equality constraint removes one degree of freedom from the decision variables. With N stocks and 2 constraints, N minus 2 degrees of freedom remain, too many to solve by inspection once N grows past 2 or 3.
Chapter 2 explains exactly why convexity is the property that makes this problem solvable and guarantees the solution you find is the true global minimum, not a local trap.
